P-CMAP-3 with the rook moved from e1 to a1, so the knight is not pinned
constructed with python-chess: White queen on d2 with rook behind on d1 against the d5 pawn

items.prompt: Black to move. Turn on the control map and tap d5. Which side does the map favour on d5, counting only the number of attackers?
hints: Read the two numbers on d5: White's count, then Black's.
Which pieces of each colour can see d5? The black queen is behind its own d7 pawn.
White has the e4 pawn and the c4 bishop; Black has only the f6 knight.
items.explain: The map shows 2-1 on d5: the e4 pawn and the c4 bishop for White, the f6 knight for Black. More White attackers means a blue tint. The map counts attackers only; it does not say who wins an exchange there.

items.prompt: Black to move. Among d5, f7, e5, g5 and h5, tap every square where White's number on the map is higher than Black's. Ignore other squares.
hints: Work square by square: write White's number, then Black's.
Some of the five are level, and one has a higher Black number.
Count how many of the five show a blue tint.
items.explain: Blue squares are those where White's count beats Black's: d5 (2-1), f7 (2-1). The others are level or favour Black.

items.prompt: Black to move. The map shows f3 as 0-1: one Black attacker, the knight on e5. Can that knight actually capture the white knight on f3? Predict, then check.

claims.statement: Ne5xf3 is illegal because the knight is pinned to its king by the rook on e1.

hints: The map counts a piece as an attacker if it attacks the square in principle.
Look along the e-file from the rook to the black king.
The e5 knight stands between them.
items.explain: The map shows 1 Black attacker on f3, but the knight on e5 is pinned to its king by the rook on e1, so it has no legal moves. The map ignores pins on purpose.

items.prompt: Black to move. The map shows f3 as 0-1: one Black attacker, the knight on e5. Can that knight capture the white knight on f3? Predict, then check.
hints: Is anything pinned? Check the lines from the white rook.
The rook is on a1, off the e-file.
Nothing stands between the knight and the capture.
items.explain: The map shows the same 0-1 on f3 here, and this time the count is real: with the rook on a1 the knight is free to capture on f3. Same map, different truth.

items.prompt: White queen on d2, White rook on d1 behind it, Black pawn on d5. How many White attackers does the map count on d5?
hints: The map counts pieces that attack the square directly.
Which White piece has a clear line to d5?
The rook is behind the queen on the same file.
items.explain: The map counts 1: only the queen attacks d5 directly. The rook behind it joins the attack once the queen has moved or captured, but the map does not show such x-rays, so you add them by looking.

items.prompt: White to move is thinking of moving the f3 knight to d4, g5 or h4. On the map as it is now, tap the squares among those three where Black has at least one attacker. (The map shows the position before you move.)
hints: For each landing square read Black's number only.
Which black pieces look at d4 from c6 and e5?
Check whether any black piece reaches g5 or h4.
items.explain: On the map d4 shows Black's number as 2 (the c6 knight and the e5 pawn); g5 and h4 show 0 for Black. A landing square with a Black number above zero deserves a second look before you move.

items.prompt: White to move. Look at the three White pieces standing on e4, c4 and f3. Tap each one whose square shows a higher Black number than White number on the map.
hints: For an occupied square, the other side's number counts the attackers and the owner's number the defenders.
Compare the two numbers on each of the three squares.
Only one White piece is attacked more than it is defended.
items.explain: The map shows the e4 pawn at 0-1: attacked by the f6 knight and defended by nothing. The c4 bishop is not attacked, and the f3 knight is defended twice and not attacked. The map shows the situation; what to do about it is a separate decision.
